abstract: Gaussian approximations to demographic noise are usually justified by large numbers of cells. In populations described by branching processes, however, a large population descended from few founders is not approximately Gaussian. A culture grown from few cells can contain thousands of cells yet retain large, skewed variation from its earliest divisions, deaths, and phenotypic switches. A random establishment amplitude, the limit of the population size divided by its exponential growth factor, summarizes this variation. We propose a founder-aware likelihood for cell cultures observed at an endpoint. Given the establishment amplitude, it approximates the remaining demographic fluctuations by a Gaussian distribution and then averages over the distribution of the amplitude. Its conditional Gaussian approximation requires a large population rather than many founders, and the likelihood approaches a single Gaussian distribution as the founder count grows. We compare it with a population Gaussian likelihood developed for many-founder cultures, using a pure-birth (Yule) process, whose cell-count distribution is known exactly, and exact simulations of a two-type process with division, death, and reversible switching. With one founder per culture, the founder-aware likelihood estimates rates more accurately than the population Gaussian likelihood, and its confidence sets are longer but have coverage close to the nominal level. With 50 founders per culture, the two likelihoods perform comparably. Founder-aware likelihoods thus suit clonal and other few-founder experiments.
